statement: In 2,019 tabulated admissions (of 2,222) to one Australian regional toxicology unit after an overdose that included a serotonergic drug (1987 to 2002), the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria, a rule built from seven bedside findings, compared with Sternbach's older criteria applied to the same records, agreed with the unit's own toxicologists' diagnosis of serotonin toxicity as follows: the new rule flagged 145 of the 172 people they diagnosed (84%; editors' 95% interval 78 to 89) and left 1,785 of the 1,847 they did not diagnose unflagged (97%; 95.7 to 97.4), against 129 of 172 (75%; 68 to 81) and 1,772 of 1,847 (96%; 94.9 to 96.7) for Sternbach's criteria; the paper gives no intervals and no test of the difference. In the presence of a serotonergic drug the rule says yes for clonus (rhythmic muscle jerks) that starts by itself; clonus that can be set off, or clonus of the eyes, together with agitation or sweating; tremor with brisk reflexes; or stiff muscles with a temperature above 38 °C and clonus of the eyes or that can be set off. The authors and two later narrative reviews (Boyer and Shannon, 2005; Buckley et al., 2014) describe serotonin toxicity as a spectrum from mild to life-threatening, caused by too much serotonin activity in the brain, with changes in muscles and nerves (shaking, brisk reflexes, clonus and, when severe, rigidity), in automatic body functions (sweating, fast heart rate, fever) and in mental state (agitation, confusion). Of 473 single-SSRI overdoses, 73 (15.4%, 95% CI 12.3 to 19.0) were diagnosed; 6 people were put on a ventilator solely because the toxicity was worsening, all with a high fever, and increasing rigidity that impaired breathing was what led to the ventilation. The authors say a fast heart rate and wide pupils were common but also occur in other poisonings, so they are poor at telling serotonin excess apart. These were overdose admissions, so the findings do not show how the signs look at prescribed amounts or in people who are never admitted to a toxicology unit; the rule was fitted to single-SSRI overdoses that are part of the test set, so the figures may be higher than they would be in new patients; 203 admissions are missing from the main table without explanation; and the diagnosis they were scored against is the unit's own judgment, which the authors call arbitrary because there is no gold standard. Later reviews call the criteria validated while citing only this paper (Buckley et al., 2014), or call the toxicologist's diagnosis a gold standard (Boyer and Shannon, 2005); no independent test is in the sources read. Early or mild signs may be taken for ordinary drug effects (Silins et al., 2007, without data).
plain: Serotonin toxicity (also called serotonin syndrome) means too much serotonin activity in the body, caused by drugs that raise serotonin. Doctors recognise it by examining the person. They look for muscle jerks that start on their own or can be set off (also in the eyes) together with agitation or sweating, for shaking with very brisk reflexes, and, in severe cases, for stiff muscles with a high fever. In one Australian hospital unit, a checklist of these signs picked out about 84 of every 100 people the unit's toxicologists had diagnosed, against about 75 in 100 for an older checklist, and left about 97 of every 100 people not diagnosed unflagged. But the standard was the unit's own judgment, the checklist was built on the same kind of patients it was tested on, and everyone had taken an overdose, so it may do less well in other settings. Mild signs can look like the ordinary effects of a drug. No independent test of the checklist was found in the papers read.
population: People admitted to one Australian regional toxicology unit (Hunter Area Toxicology Service, Newcastle, New South Wales) from 13 January 1987 to 22 November 2002 after an overdose that included at least one serotonergic drug: 2,222 of 9,960 admissions, of which 2,019 are in the main accuracy table; the rule was built from the 473 admissions with an overdose of one SSRI alone, which are part of the 2,222. Ages, sex, the drugs taken and the amounts are not reported. Descriptions of what serotonin toxicity is come from the paper and from two narrative reviews.
exposure: The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria applied to the admission record: in the presence of a serotonergic agent, yes if spontaneous clonus; inducible clonus with agitation or sweating; ocular clonus with agitation or sweating; tremor with brisk reflexes; or stiff muscles with a temperature above 38 °C and ocular or inducible clonus; otherwise no
comparator: Sternbach's 1991 criteria (three or more of ten listed features, with a recent addition or increase of a serotonergic agent) applied to the same records; both sets of criteria scored against the diagnosis made by the admitting clinical toxicologist, with treatment by a 5-HT2A antagonist and Sternbach's criteria as two further reference outcomes
outcome: Agreement with the admitting toxicologist's diagnosis of serotonin toxicity (sensitivity and specificity); how often that diagnosis was made in single-SSRI overdoses; and the findings of the six people ventilated solely for worsening toxicity
magnitude: Test set against the toxicologist's diagnosis (Table 1a; 2,019 of 2,222 admissions, the other 203 not in the table): flagged and diagnosed 145; flagged but not diagnosed 62; not flagged but diagnosed 27; not flagged and not diagnosed 1,785 (172 diagnosed, 1,847 not diagnosed). Printed sensitivity 84% and specificity 97%. Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% intervals; the paper gives none): sensitivity 84.3% (78.1 to 89.0); specificity 96.6% (95.7 to 97.4); positive predictive value 145/207 = 70.0% (63.5 to 75.9); negative predictive value 1,785/1,812 = 98.5% (97.8 to 99.0). Sternbach's criteria on the same records (Table 2): 1,772, 75, 43 and 129; printed sensitivity 75% and specificity 96%; editors' calculation from the cells: 129/172 = 75.0% (68.0 to 80.9) and 1,772/1,847 = 95.9% (94.9 to 96.7); positive predictive value 129/204 = 63.2% from the cells (69.4% if the printed column total of 186 is used). Against Sternbach's criteria as the reference (Table 1b) the Hunter rule had printed sensitivity 69% and specificity 97%; against treatment with a 5-HT2A antagonist (Table 1c) 78% and 94%. No test is given for the difference between the two sets of criteria; the editors' intervals for sensitivity overlap, and the people are the same in both. Derivation set (473 single-SSRI overdoses): diagnosed by a toxicologist 73 (15.4%, 95% CI 12.3 to 19.0); met Sternbach's criteria 70 (14.8%, 11.7 to 18.4); treated with a 5-HT2A antagonist 44 (9.3%, 6.8 to 12.3). Intubated: 42 for reduced consciousness or decontamination and 6 solely for worsening serotonin toxicity (6 of 2,222 = 0.27%, editors' calculation).

evidence.extracted: Figure 2, decision rules: in the presence of a serotonergic agent, serotonin toxicity is yes if (1) spontaneous clonus; (2) inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; (3) ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; (4) tremor with hyperreflexia; or (5) hypertonic with a temperature above 38 C and ocular or inducible clonus; otherwise no. Seven variables were needed: spontaneous, inducible and ocular clonus, agitation, diaphoresis, tremor and hyperreflexia. Rule 5 was added although the classification-tree analysis did not select it, because clonus and hyperreflexia are often not demonstrable in severe rigidity; the life-threatening cases were not in the learning dataset of SSRI-alone overdoses, because they occur with combinations of serotonergic agents.

Table 1a, Hunter rule against the toxicologist's diagnosis: not diagnosed and not flagged 1785; not diagnosed but flagged 62; diagnosed but not flagged 27; diagnosed and flagged 145; row totals 1847 and 172, column totals 1812 and 207, 2019 in the table; printed sensitivity 84% and specificity 97%. Table 1b, Sternbach's criteria as the reference: 1951, 67, 64, 140; printed 69% and 97%. Table 1c, treatment with a 5-HT2A antagonist as the reference: 1991, 124, 24, 83; printed 78% and 94%. The grand total of Table 1b is printed as 222. Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% intervals; the paper gives none): sensitivity 145/172 = 84.3% (78.1 to 89.0); specificity 1785/1847 = 96.6% (95.7 to 97.4); positive predictive value 145/207 = 70.0% (63.5 to 75.9); negative predictive value 1785/1812 = 98.5% (97.8 to 99.0).

evidence.extracted: Table 2, Sternbach's criteria against the toxicologist's diagnosis in the same records: not diagnosed and not flagged 1772; not diagnosed but flagged 75; diagnosed but not flagged 43; diagnosed and flagged 129; printed sensitivity 75% and specificity 96%; the printed column totals (1833 and 186) do not match the cells. The paper gives no interval and no test of the difference from the Hunter rule. Editors' calculation: 129/172 = 75.0% (68.0 to 80.9); 1772/1847 = 95.9% (94.9 to 96.7); column totals from the cells 1815 and 204; positive predictive value 129/204 = 63.2%.

evidence.locator: Introduction, last paragraph (p. 637); Methods, 1st paragraph (p. 637); Methods › Derivation dataset and Test dataset (p. 638); Results, 1st paragraph and SSRI-alone overdoses, 1st paragraph (p. 638)
evidence.extracted: The Hunter Area Toxicology Service is a regional toxicology unit; every overdose presentation and admission is entered prospectively into a clinical database by two trained staff who were blind to the hypotheses. Of 9960 admissions between 13 January 1987 and 22 November 2002, 2222 involved at least one serotonergic drug taken in overdose; this test dataset had no exclusions and includes the derivation dataset. Derivation dataset: 473 admissions with a single SSRI, after excluding 9 with two SSRIs and any with a tricyclic antidepressant, MAOI, venlafaxine, nefazodone, lithium or an anti-serotonergic drug taken as well. Of the 473, 73 (15.4%, 95%CI 12.3–19.0) had a diagnosis of serotonin toxicity made by a clinical toxicologist, 70 (14.8%, 95%CI 11.7–18.4) met Sternbach's criteria and 44 (9.3%, 95%CI 6.8–12.3) were treated with a 5-HT2A antagonist. The tree analysis was done in the SSRI-alone dataset; the rules were tested on the complete dataset. The paper reports no ages, sex, drugs or amounts.

Life-threatening cases were those intubated and ventilated. Forty-two patients were intubated for a decreased Glasgow Coma Score or for decontamination; six were intubated solely for worsening serotonin toxicity. All six had a high fever and multiple features of serotonin toxicity. Progressive rigidity compromising respiratory function was the precipitating event; the preceding signs were a high fever (above 38.5 C) and increasing, particularly truncal, rigidity and peripheral hypertonicity. Editors' calculation: 6 of 2222 admissions = 0.27%.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (continues in the right-hand column, from the words The arbitrary approach taken)
evidence.extracted: The authors state that the approach was arbitrary and was mandated by the lack of a gold standard for defining clinically significant serotonin toxicity, which is a spectrum and not a discrete syndrome; they therefore used the diagnosis made by a clinical toxicologist as the standard and compared it with Sternbach's criteria and with the use of treatment.
evidence.quote: mandated by the lack of a gold standard

evidence.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning Although mydriasis occurred commonly (top of the left-hand column); Discussion, last paragraph (beginning The decision rules will need to be validated)
evidence.extracted: Mydriasis occurred in 31.6% of patients and tachycardia in 40%, but both also occur with anticholinergic and other drug toxicity (tachycardia is common in drug overdose in general), so the authors call them unlikely to be good discriminators of serotonergic excess from other toxidromes. The authors acknowledge the arbitrary nature of certain decisions in developing the criteria. They state that the decision rules will need to be validated in other settings, including other toxicology treatment centres, emergency departments and psychiatric units, and studied prospectively in people taking toxic and therapeutic amounts of serotonergic drugs.

evidence.locator: Introduction, paragraph beginning Serotonin excess is best thought of as a spectrum (right-hand column)
evidence.extracted: The authors write that serotonin excess is best thought of as a spectrum of toxicity rather than a defined clinical entity with clear prognostic importance, and so call it serotonin toxicity; that it results from an increase in serotonin in the synapses of the central nervous system, so is a concentration-dependent toxicity that can develop in any individual and not an idiosyncratic reaction; and that it can be thought of as a triad of autonomic signs, neuromuscular changes and altered mental status.

evidence.locator: Opening paragraph; Definition and epidemiology, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review calls the serotonin syndrome a potentially life-threatening adverse drug reaction, a predictable consequence of excess serotonin stimulation of receptors, with clinical manifestations from barely perceptible to lethal. It is often described as a triad of mental-status changes, autonomic hyperactivity and neuromuscular abnormalities, but not all are present in every person; signs range from tremor and diarrhoea in mild cases to delirium, neuromuscular rigidity and hyperthermia in life-threatening cases; mild symptoms may be easily overlooked.

evidence.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning To better delineate the signs and symptoms (p. 1114); Diagnosis, 2nd paragraph (p. 1115)
evidence.extracted: The review describes its source as the clinical findings in 2222 consecutive cases of self-poisoning with serotonergic drugs from a toxicology registry, compared with the gold standard of a medical toxicologist's diagnosis, and says its preferred decision rules are simpler, more sensitive (84 percent against 75 percent) and more specific (97 percent against 96 percent) than the original criteria. It does not say that the figures come from one unit or that the rules were derived in part of the same records, gives no intervals, and does not mention the source paper's statement that no gold standard exists.

evidence.locator: What is serotonin syndrome?, 1st paragraph; How does it present?, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review describes serotonin syndrome, also called serotonin toxicity, as a drug-induced cluster of dose-related adverse effects due to increased serotonin in the central nervous system, covering a spectrum from mild to severe. It says toxicity starts within hours of ingesting the drugs and that the classic triad is neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, rigidity), autonomic excitation (hyperthermia, tachycardia) and altered mental state (agitation, confusion).

evidence.locator: How do we diagnose it?, 2nd paragraph (beginning Some pathognomonic features)
evidence.extracted: The review calls generalised clonus (inducible, spontaneous, ocular) the classic feature and the key component of the Hunter criteria, which it says have been validated and can be used to confirm moderate or severe toxicity; the only source cited for this statement is the derivation paper (reference 13). It describes spontaneous clonus as rhythmic, large muscle contractions, often triggered by minor movements or vibrations and easily brought out with ankle dorsiflexion, and ocular clonus as fine or coarse oscillations of gaze in all directions.

evidence.locator: Introduction, paragraph beginning Serotonin syndrome is a drug-induced toxic state
evidence.extracted: The review says people with serotonin syndrome from illicit drugs such as ecstasy usually reach emergency departments with more advanced symptoms, because some of the early, mild signs are generally seen by many people who use ecstasy as part of normal drug reactions; it cites one earlier review for this and gives no data. It describes the typical picture as agitation or hypervigilance with tremor and exaggerated reflexes, with muscle spasms starting in the lower limbs and becoming generalised, then fever, sweating, dilated pupils, rapid heart rate and rapid breathing, and fixed rigidity in severe cases.

risk_of_bias.note: QUADAS-2 overall high on the study card: the rules were fitted to and scored on overlapping admissions (the test set contains the 473 derivation admissions), the cut points were fitted to the data, rule 5 was added by hand, and the reference diagnosis is the same unit's judgment on much the same findings; flow unclear (203 admissions missing from the main table).

inconsistency.note: Not assessable: one study; the reviews restate its figures and add no test.

indirectness.note: None as worded: the claim names the population (overdose admissions to one unit), the rule and the reference, and says it does not extend to prescribed amounts, other settings or the mixes behind the most severe cases.

imprecision.note: The claim gives the printed figures with the editors' intervals (about 11 points wide for sensitivity) and does not rank the two sets of criteria; the missing paired test is stated.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the evidence is descriptive or consists of reports, and the rating is already at the floor (METHODS 6.3).

grade.reasoning: A retrospective analysis of a prospectively collected registry starts low (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 (QUADAS-2 overall high on the card: index test and reference standard both high, flow unclear); inconsistency, indirectness (as worded), imprecision and publication bias 0. Very low. Relation: describes, because the claim reports how a rule agreed with one unit's diagnosis, not that the rule is accurate against a proven condition (the authors say there is none), so no upgrade applies. Status single study: the three later reviews read restate the figures and none tests the rules. The what-it-is description rests on the paper's introduction and two narrative reviews and is marked as described. Recognition is stated as a finding about how one set of rules performed, not as instructions.

verification.flag_note: Rests on one registry study (Dunkley et al., 2003) read in full; the descriptions of what serotonin toxicity is come from its introduction and two narrative reviews (Boyer and Shannon 2005; Buckley et al. 2014), marked as described. Pair chosen for display: the claim serves the opioid pair too (the editor may show it in both). No independent test of the Hunter criteria was found among the six papers read; the literature outside them was not searched. Isbister et al. 2003 (Br J Clin Pharmacol 56:441-50, moclobemide poisoning), cited by Dunkley, Gillman and Buckley, has no reference record and was not read. Treatment and first-aid statements in the sources (doses, antagonists, admission) are not used.
